analysis.one_liner: Makes big-bank executives personally certify disclosed crimes and fraud, with criminal penalties.
analysis.headline: Senator Warren's bill to create a permanent bank-crime watchdog died in committee with no cosponsors and never reached a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would convert the temporary bank-bailout watchdog (SIGTARP) into a permanent office dedicated to investigating fraud at financial institutions. It would require the CEO, CFO, COO, and chief compliance officer of any bank, bank holding company, or savings and loan holding company with more than $10 billion in assets to personally certify each year that all criminal conduct and civil fraud has been disclosed to the Justice Department — with civil fines up to $25,000 and criminal penalties up to 10 years in prison for willful violations. It would also require a court to find that a deferred prosecution agreement with a corporation is in the public interest before approving it, and to publish such agreements online.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors, taxpayers, and investors: the bill targets the fraud by bank insiders that the 2008 crisis exposed and that the record cites as causing an estimated $7 billion in losses to the deposit insurance fund. Personal certification puts executives — not just shareholders — on the hook, and a permanent investigative office would keep hunting bank fraud after the bailout-era watchdog expires.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent office (renamed from SIGTARP) whose sole duty is investigating fraudulent conduct in or impacting financial institutions, bank holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies [S2][S3].

Requires the CEO, CFO, COO, and chief compliance officer of any such institution over $10 billion in assets to certify annually, under penalty of perjury, that all criminal conduct and civil fraud has been fully disclosed to the Justice Department or regulators [S2][S3].

Imposes civil penalties (up to $25,000 for willful violations) and criminal penalties (up to $250,000 in fines and 5 years in prison, up to $500,000 and 10 years in aggravated cases) on executives who willfully violate the certification requirement [S3].

Requires courts to find a deferred prosecution agreement with a corporation is in the public interest — weighing whether reforms prevent repeat conduct and penalties compensate victims — and to post such agreements and monitor terms publicly [S2][S3].

The bill's findings note SIGTARP investigations produced criminal charges against more than 400 defendants, including nearly 100 bankers, tied to more than 20 failed banks with about $7 billion in losses to the deposit insurance fund [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and their top executives: compliance costs to run due-diligence programs and file annual certifications, and — for executives at institutions where wrongdoing was concealed — real personal exposure to fines and prison. The public cost is funding the permanent watchdog office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and their top executives

drawbacks.text: The annual certification duplicates existing disclosure duties: officers already certify financial statements under Sarbanes-Oxley, and banks already face criminal referral obligations, so the marginal deterrence may be smaller than it appears [S3].

Requiring every CEO and CFO at hundreds of institutions over $10 billion to swear there is no undisclosed misconduct creates legal risk for executives over conduct they may have no practical ability to detect inside large organizations [S3].
Requiring judicial approval of deferred prosecution agreements could slow the plea and settlement process prosecutors use to resolve corporate cases quickly and extract reforms [S3].
The modest civil penalties ($25,000 willful, $500 negligent) are small relative to bank revenues, so the bill's teeth depend mostly on the criminal provisions and on DOJ following through [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — putting named executives personally on the legal hook for their bank's undisclosed crimes, and keeping a proven fraud-hunting office permanent — is real and aimed at a documented problem: the bill's own findings cite nearly 100 bankers criminally charged after bank failures costing the deposit insurance fund an estimated $7 billion. The compliance burden falls on institutions with assets over $10 billion, for which annual certifications are a modest cost. The honest objection is that the certification regime may add paperwork without changing conduct unless regulators and DOJ actually use the enforcement tools, and the judicial review of deferred prosecution agreements is untested. On balance the costs fall on the industry the bill polices and the benefit runs to the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2019, got no cosponsors, no hearing or markup, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on April 3, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
No senator ever cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list shows zero [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no vote, the Senate never debated it, and the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and their senior executives, who face no new personal certification duties, penalties, or exposure to the permanent bank-fraud watchdog the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks and their senior executives

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only supporter in the Senate; it never advanced past referral.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Mike Crapo, R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and it sat in the majority-controlled Banking Committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors of either party, so no formal partisan split was ever recorded; it died in the Republican-controlled Banking Committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Large banks, bank holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies (over $10 billion in assets)
industries.note: Their top four officers would have to personally certify — under threat of fines and up to 10 years in prison — that all criminal conduct and civil fraud was disclosed to the Justice Department, and a permanent watchdog would investigate fraud in or impacting them. The bill's entire purpose is to remove the practical shield large institutions have enjoyed when wrongdoing is settled with corporate fines rather than prosecuted.

industries.industry: Corporations that settle federal charges through deferred prosecution agreements
industries.note: Courts would have to find each agreement is in the public interest — weighing repeat conduct and victim compensation — and the agreements and monitor terms would be posted publicly, ending the confidentiality these deals currently enjoy.
